Guide

What to introduce, and when

There is no mandatory calendar of single vegetables. There is a reason to bring allergens in early and to keep them in the diet.

Findings

A one-food-at-a-time ladder is a habit, not a rule. New allergens are easier to read if they arrive one at a time. Ordinary vegetables do not need three days of isolation.
Gluten can come in with the first solids. Delaying it does not prevent coeliac disease. Very large amounts in the first weeks are worth avoiding.
Whole cow’s milk is not the main drink before one year. Small amounts in a sauce, a porridge, or a yogurt are fine from the start of solids.

Drop the long ladder

Older weaning charts offered one new vegetable every few days and held meat, wheat, egg, and fish until late in the first year. That pattern made diaries tidy and iron intake poor. It also missed the window in which early allergen introduction appears to protect.

Introduce one new common allergen on a morning when the baby is well, in a small amount, and watch. The next day you can repeat it. Other new foods, such as a different vegetable, can share the plate. If there is no reaction, keep the allergen in the diet several times a week. A single taste does not maintain tolerance.

Gluten, egg, fish, and the rest

ESPGHAN says gluten may be introduced between 4 and 12 months, and that large quantities should be avoided in the first weeks after introduction and through infancy. A portion of pasta or bread is appropriate. A stack of biscuits is not.

Egg should be fully cooked. Fish should be boneless and fully cooked. Peanut and other nuts should be smooth butter, thinned, never whole and never a dense spoonful. Sesame is tahini, not a sprinkle of whole seeds. Details and the high-risk peanut pathway are on the allergen page.

Milk as a drink and milk as a food

Breast milk or infant formula remains the main drink until 12 months. Whole cow’s milk as that drink raises the risk of a poor iron intake and is not a formula substitute. After the first birthday, whole cow’s milk can become the drink, at roughly 350 to 400 ml a day so it does not crowd out meals.

Yogurt, pasteurised cheese in small amounts, and milk in a cooked sauce are foods, not drinks. They are reasonable from six months. Unpasteurised milk and mould-ripened or blue cheeses stay out of the first years.
